title: How Airplanes Fly
summary: How a plane's curved wings, its engines, and the pilot's controls work together to lift a heavy aircraft into the sky and keep it there.
poll: Flying in an airplane is one of the safest ways to travel.

versions.title: How Planes Stay Up in the Air
versions.text:
Look at a big plane. It is heavy. But it flies!

A plane has two wings. Air moves over the wings fast.

A plane has an engine too. The engine pushes the plane. It makes the plane go fast.

Air moves over the wing. This makes lift. Lift pushes the plane up.

A pilot sits at the front. The pilot flies the plane.

Long ago, two brothers made the first plane. Their names were Orville and Wilbur Wright. It flew for just twelve seconds. That was in 1903.

Today, big planes fly high in the air. They carry many people far away.

A plane has an engine too. The engine pushes the plane forward through the air.

Air moves over the wing. This makes lift. Lift is a force that pushes the plane up into the sky.

A pilot sits at the front of the plane. The pilot flies the plane and keeps it safe.

Today, big planes fly high in the air. They carry many people far away, above the clouds.

versions.title: How Planes Stay Up in the Air
versions.text:
Look at a big, heavy plane. It seems hard to believe, but it can fly!

A plane has two long wings. Each wing has a curved top. Air moves over the wings fast when the plane speeds up.

A plane has at least one engine. The engine pushes the plane forward through the air very fast.

As air moves over the curved wing, a force called lift is made. Lift pushes up on the wing, and the plane rises into the sky.

A pilot sits at the front of the plane. The pilot controls the engine and the wings to keep the flight safe.

Long ago, in 1903, two brothers made the first flying machine that really worked. Their names were Orville and Wilbur Wright. Their first flight lasted only twelve seconds.

Today, big planes fly high above the clouds. They carry many people far away, from country to country.

versions.title: How Airplanes Fly
versions.text:
Look at a big, heavy plane lifting off the ground. It seems hard to believe, but it happens every day at busy airports.

A plane has two long wings, and each wing has a curved top. Air moves over the wings fast when the plane speeds up.

A plane has an engine, which pushes it forward very fast through the air. As air moves over the curved wing, a force called lift is made. Lift pushes up on the wing. If there is enough lift, the whole plane rises into the sky.

A pilot sits at the front and carefully controls the engine, the wings, and the tail. Small moving parts on the wings and tail help the pilot turn and land safely.

Long ago, in 1903, two brothers made the first flying machine that really worked, at a windy beach in North Carolina. Their names were Orville and Wilbur Wright. Their first flight lasted only about twelve seconds.

Today, big planes fly high above the clouds. They carry many people between countries, even across oceans, in just a few hours of flying time.

versions.title: How Airplanes Fly
versions.text:
A heavy airplane roaring down a runway and lifting into the sky seems almost magical. It happens at busy airports every single day. Engineers understand the science behind it quite well.

Every plane depends on four forces working together. Gravity pulls the plane down toward the earth. Lift, an upward force, must be strong enough to beat gravity. The engines make thrust, a forward push that moves the plane through the air. Drag, a backward force from air, tries to slow the plane down.

The wings make lift possible because of their curved shape. As the plane speeds up, air flows over and under each wing, and this makes the wing push up into the sky.

Inside the cockpit at the front, the pilot controls the engines and the parts on the wings and tail. The pilot adjusts speed, altitude, and direction during the flight. This keeps everyone safe.

In 1903, two brothers, Orville and Wilbur Wright, made the first powered flight near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Their flight lasted only twelve seconds and covered about 120 feet.

Today, big jets fly at a high altitude. They carry hundreds of passengers across oceans in just a few hours of flying time.

versions.title: How Airplanes Fly
versions.text:
A heavy airplane roaring down a runway and lifting into the sky seems almost magical. It happens at busy airports every single day around the world, and the underlying science has been well understood by engineers for more than a century.

Every plane depends on four forces working together throughout a flight. Gravity pulls the plane down toward the earth. Lift, an upward force, must be strong enough to beat gravity at every moment. The engines make thrust, a forward push that moves the plane through the air. Drag, a backward force caused by air resistance, constantly tries to slow the plane down.

The wings make lift possible because of their special curved shape. As the plane gains speed, air flows over and under each wing, and this difference in pressure makes the wing push up into the sky.

Before engineers build a real wing, they often test smaller models inside a wind tunnel, a machine that blows air past the model to study exactly how it performs under different conditions. Inside the cockpit at the front, the pilot controls the engines and the moving parts on the wings and tail, carefully adjusting speed, altitude, and direction throughout the entire flight.

In 1903, two American brothers, Orville and Wilbur Wright, achieved the first powered flight near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Their flight lasted only twelve seconds and covered roughly 120 feet, using a flimsy frame built mostly of wood and cloth.

Today, modern jets are built largely of lightweight aluminum. They fly at a high cruising altitude and carry hundreds of passengers across entire oceans in just a matter of hours, in great comfort and safety.

versions.title: How Airplanes Fly
versions.text:
A heavy airplane roaring down a runway and lifting into the sky seems almost magical, yet the underlying aerodynamic science has been well understood by engineers for more than a century.

Every plane depends on four forces working together throughout a flight. Gravity pulls the plane down toward the earth, while lift, an upward force, must be strong enough to overcome it. The engines generate thrust, a forward push that drives the plane through the atmosphere, while drag, a backward force caused by air resistance, works to slow the plane down.

The wings make lift possible because of their curved cross-section. As the plane gains speed, air flows over and under each wing, and this difference in pressure pushes the wing upward into the sky.

Pilots adjust several moving surfaces to control the aircraft with precision. Ailerons near the wingtips tilt the plane left or right, while a rudder and elevators mounted on the tail control turning and climbing or descending. Engineers also test wing models inside a wind tunnel before building a real one, to study how each design performs.

Orville and Wilbur Wright, two pioneering American brothers, achieved the first powered, controlled flight near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903. Their historic flight lasted only twelve seconds and covered roughly 120 feet, using a fragile frame built mostly of wood and cloth, yet it changed transportation forever.

Modern jets are built largely of lightweight aluminum and advanced composite materials, and their cabins are pressurized so passengers can breathe comfortably at a high cruising altitude, far above where unprotected air would be too thin to breathe safely. Crossing entire oceans in only a few hours, these aircraft have made distant countries feel remarkably close together.

Even with countless safe flights every single day, engineers keep studying the forces of flight, hoping to make future aircraft lighter, quieter, and more efficient than ever before.

versions.title: How Airplanes Fly
versions.text:
A massive airplane thundering down a runway and lifting smoothly into the sky seems almost magical, yet the underlying aerodynamic science has been thoroughly understood by engineers for more than a century.

Every aircraft depends on four forces working together throughout a flight. Gravity continuously pulls the plane downward toward the earth, while lift, an upward force, must be sufficiently strong to overcome it. The engines generate thrust, a forward force that propels the plane through the atmosphere, while drag, a backward force caused by air resistance, constantly works to slow the aircraft down.

The wings make lift possible because of their specially curved cross-section, known to engineers as an airfoil. As the plane accelerates, air flows over and under each wing, and this difference in pressure pushes the wing steadily upward.

Pilots adjust several movable surfaces to control the aircraft with considerable precision. Ailerons positioned near the wingtips tilt the plane left or right, while a rudder and elevators mounted on the tail govern turning and climbing or descending. Engineers also test smaller wing models inside a wind tunnel, studying precisely how each design will perform under varied conditions.

Orville and Wilbur Wright, two pioneering American brothers, spent years testing unpowered gliders before achieving the first powered, controlled flight near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903. Their historic flight lasted only twelve seconds and covered roughly 120 feet, using a fragile frame constructed mostly of wood and cloth, yet it transformed transportation forever.

Modern jets are built largely of lightweight aluminum and advanced composite materials, which combine considerable strength with remarkably low weight. Their cabins are pressurized so that passengers can breathe comfortably at a high cruising altitude, far above where the thin outside atmosphere would otherwise prove impossible to breathe. Crossing entire oceans in only a matter of hours, these remarkable aircraft have made distant countries feel astonishingly close together.

Engineers continue to study these same four forces today, refining wing shapes and engine designs so that future aircraft can fly farther while burning less fuel and producing noticeably less noise as they pass far overhead above the clouds.

The engines generate thrust, a forward force that propels the plane through the atmosphere, while drag, a backward force caused by air resistance, constantly works to slow the aircraft down.

versions.title: How Airplanes Fly
versions.text:
A massive airplane thundering down a runway and lifting smoothly into the open sky seems almost magical, yet the underlying aerodynamic science has been thoroughly and rigorously understood by engineers for well over a century now.

Every aircraft depends upon four distinct forces working together in careful, continuous balance throughout a flight. Gravity continuously pulls the plane downward toward the earth, while lift, an upward force, must be sufficiently strong to overcome it at every single moment. The engines generate thrust, a forward force that propels the plane through the atmosphere, while drag, a backward force caused by air resistance, constantly works to slow the aircraft down considerably.

The wings make lift possible because of their specially curved cross-section, known to engineers as an airfoil. As the plane accelerates, air flows over and under each wing, and this difference in pressure pushes the wing steadily, predictably upward.

Pilots adjust several movable surfaces to control the aircraft with considerable precision. Ailerons positioned near the wingtips tilt the plane left or right, while a rudder and elevators mounted on the tail govern turning and climbing or descending. Engineers also test smaller wing models inside a wind tunnel, studying precisely how each design will perform under widely varied conditions before it ever leaves the ground.

Orville and Wilbur Wright, two pioneering American brothers, spent years patiently testing unpowered gliders before finally achieving the first powered, controlled flight near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903. Their historic flight lasted a mere twelve seconds and covered roughly 120 feet, using a fragile frame constructed mostly of wood and cloth, yet it transformed transportation forever and inspired countless generations of later engineers and pioneers around the world.

Modern jets are built largely of lightweight aluminum and advanced composite materials, which combine considerable structural strength with remarkably low weight. Their cabins are pressurized so that passengers can breathe comfortably at a high cruising altitude, far above where the thin outside atmosphere would otherwise prove entirely impossible to breathe safely for very long at all. At such extreme altitudes, engines must also be meticulously designed to keep functioning efficiently in air that is considerably thinner than at ground level.

Crossing entire oceans in only a matter of hours, these remarkable aircraft have made distant countries feel astonishingly close together, even though, at any given moment, countless redundant safety systems are quietly and continuously working to keep every single flight secure. Engineers continue to study these same four forces today, meticulously refining wing shapes, engine designs, and even the composite materials themselves, so that future aircraft can fly farther while burning considerably less fuel and producing far less noise.

Furthermore, although the fundamental principles governing lift, thrust, drag, and gravity have remained essentially unchanged since the Wright brothers' pioneering achievement, the materials, instrumentation, and computational modeling techniques available to contemporary aerospace engineers have advanced so dramatically that today's aircraft bear remarkably little structural resemblance to that fragile wood-and-cloth biplane from 1903.

keyWords.example: Engineers pressurize a submarine's cabin so the crew can breathe safely underwater.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of this article?
options: Flight comes from four balanced forces and a wing's airfoil shape, refined by engineers since 1903.
Ailerons are no longer used on any modern passenger planes flying in the sky today anywhere.
The Wright brothers' original fragile 1903 biplane is still flown every single day.
Composite materials make modern planes much heavier than wood and cloth ever did.
questions.why: The article traces flight from the four forces and the airfoil shape through the Wright brothers' pioneering flight to today's pressurized, composite-built jets.

wrong.B: The article says modern pilots still use ailerons to control the aircraft.
wrong.C: The original 1903 aircraft is not described as still in use.
wrong.D: Composite materials are strong and light, not heavy.

questions.stem: What do ailerons do?
options: They pressurize the cabin
They tilt the plane left or right
They measure altitude
They test models in a wind tunnel
questions.why: The article says ailerons near the wingtips tilt the plane left or right.

wrong.A: Cabin pressure is a separate system.
wrong.C: Measuring altitude is not described as the ailerons' job.
wrong.D: Wind tunnels test wing models; they are not part of the aileron's job.

questions.stem: What were the Wright brothers' first flying machine's wings and frame built from?
options: Aluminum and steel
Glass and rubber
Wood and cloth
Composite materials
questions.why: In the article, their fragile frame was constructed mostly of wood and cloth.

wrong.A: Aluminum is described as a later, modern material.
wrong.B: Glass and rubber are not mentioned.
wrong.D: Composite materials are described as used in modern jets, not the 1903 aircraft.

questions.stem: In the article, what does atmosphere mean?
options: A force that pulls a plane down to the ground
A part of the cockpit in the plane
A kind of composite material used to make wings
The layer of air surrounding the earth
questions.why: The article uses atmosphere to describe the layer of air a plane flies through, which becomes thin at high altitude.

wrong.A: That describes gravity, a different force.
wrong.B: The cockpit is a separate part of the plane.
wrong.C: Composite material is a different concept entirely.

questions.stem: Why must airplane cabins be pressurized at a high cruising altitude?
options: Because the outside atmosphere is too thin to breathe safely at that height
Because gravity becomes noticeably stronger way up at high altitude
Because the ailerons simply stop working without enough air pressure
Because composite materials need extra pressure just to stay strong
questions.why: In the article, cabins are pressurized because the thin outside atmosphere at cruising altitude would otherwise be impossible to breathe safely.

wrong.B: The article does not say gravity changes with altitude.
wrong.C: Ailerons are not linked to cabin pressure.
wrong.D: Composite material strength is not linked to cabin pressure.

questions.stem: Why do engineers test wing models in a wind tunnel before building a real plane?
options: To paint the small test model many different bright colors so it looks nice for visitors and children
To check how the design will perform in the air before committing to a full-sized version
To deliberately make the small test model noticeably heavier than before so it falls faster
To completely and permanently replace the need for a trained human pilot in every plane
questions.why: Testing a smaller model in a wind tunnel lets engineers study how a wing design will perform before building the real, full-sized version.

wrong.A: Painting is not mentioned.
wrong.C: Adding weight is not the purpose described.
wrong.D: The article still describes a pilot controlling the finished aircraft.

questions.stem: How are composite materials different from the wood and cloth used by the Wright brothers?
options: Composite materials are heavier but noticeably weaker overall than wood
Composite materials are weaker but much, much cheaper to produce
Composite materials combine strength with much lower weight
Composite materials cannot easily be shaped into wings at all, ever
questions.why: Composite materials are both strong and very light, unlike the weak wood-and-cloth frame of 1903.

wrong.A: The article describes composites as light, not heavy.
wrong.B: Cost is not compared in the article.
wrong.D: Composite materials are described as used in building modern jets, including their structure.

questions.stem: How does the article mainly trace the story of flight?
options: By arguing that modern jets are unsafe, and then by showing how to fix them.
By comparing ticket prices across different airlines and the cost of each flight for families on holiday.
By listing the names of famous pilots, with a short story about each of them.
By moving from the forces and shape that create flight to its history and today's technology
questions.why: The article explains the forces and airfoil shape first, then the Wright brothers' pioneering flight, then today's composite, pressurized jets.

wrong.A: The article mentions redundant safety systems, not a lack of safety.
wrong.B: Ticket prices are not discussed.
wrong.C: No list of famous pilots' names appears.

HIGH.prompt: The article says flight depends on both scientific forces and historical innovation. Explain one scientific fact and one historical fact from the article, and how they connect.
checklist: I explained one scientific fact and one historical fact.
I showed how the two facts connect.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Scientifically, a wing's curved airfoil shape creates lift by making air pressure differ above and below the wing, and this lift must overcome gravity for a plane to fly. Historically, Orville and Wilbur Wright, two pioneering brothers, proved this science could work when their fragile wood-and-cloth aircraft achieved the first powered, controlled flight in 1903. That twelve-second flight connects directly to today's composite, pressurized jets, since every modern aircraft still relies on the same basic forces the Wright brothers first harnessed.

LOW.stem: What does the engine do for the plane?
options: It makes the wings
It sits at the front
It makes the air cold
It pushes the plane
LOW.why: The engine pushes the plane and makes it go fast.

wrong.A: The text says the plane has two wings but does not say the engine makes them.
wrong.B: The pilot sits at the front, not the engine.
wrong.C: The text never says the engine makes air cold.

LOW.stem: In the article, who is the pilot?
options: A boy riding on a bike
The one who flies the plane
A man who builds the wings
A guide at a big airport
LOW.why: In the text, the pilot sits at the front and flies the plane.

wrong.A: The text never mentions a bike.
wrong.C: The Wright brothers made a plane, but the pilot flies it.
wrong.D: The text does not mention airport guides.

LOW.stem: What makes lift for a plane?
options: Air moving fast over the wing
The plane sitting still on land
The pilot jumping up and down
Two brothers pushing the wing
LOW.why: The text says air moves over the wing and this makes lift.

wrong.B: A plane sitting still has no air moving over its wings.
wrong.C: The text does not say the pilot makes lift.
wrong.D: The Wright brothers built the first plane, but they do not make lift.

LOW.stem: Why does a plane need both wings and an engine?
options: The wings make it very heavy
The engine helps the pilot to see
Wings lift it and the engine pushes
The engine holds the plane down
LOW.why: The wings help make lift and the engine pushes the plane fast, so both help it fly.

wrong.A: The text says the plane is heavy but does not say wings cause this.
wrong.B: The engine pushes the plane and has nothing to do with seeing.
wrong.D: Lift pushes the plane up, so nothing holds it down here.

MID.stem: Where did the Wright brothers make their first powered flight?
options: Near an ocean in Spain
Near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina
Near a busy airport in Texas
Near a hill in Paris
MID.why: In the text, the flight was made near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.

wrong.A: Spain is not mentioned.
wrong.C: The text does not say the flight was near an airport.
wrong.D: Paris is not mentioned in the text.

MID.stem: In the article, what does the word thrust mean?
options: A backward force from air
A force that pulls things down
The tail part of a plane
A forward push
MID.why: The text says the engines make thrust, a forward push.

wrong.A: That describes drag.
wrong.B: That describes gravity.
wrong.C: Thrust is a force, not a part of the plane.

MID.stem: What would happen if lift were weaker than gravity?
options: The plane could not rise
The plane would fly faster
The pilot would feel no drag
The engines would stop
MID.why: The text says lift must be strong enough to beat gravity, so weak lift would not lift the plane.

wrong.B: Speed is not linked to weak lift in the text.
wrong.C: Drag comes from air, not from lift.
wrong.D: The text does not say the engines stop.

MID.stem: Why does the author say flight seems almost magical?
options: To say that flight is not really science
To teach readers how to fly a jet
To show how amazing flight feels
To warn readers that flying is not safe
MID.why: The author calls flight almost magical and then explains that engineers understand the science.

wrong.A: In the text, engineers understand the science well.
wrong.B: The article does not teach readers to fly a jet.
wrong.D: The article does not warn that flying is unsafe.

HIGH.stem: What do the rudder and elevators on the tail control?
options: Turning and climbing or descending
The tilt of the wingtips in the air
The pressure inside the cabin
The strength of the plane engines
HIGH.why: The text says the rudder and elevators on the tail control turning and climbing or descending.

wrong.B: Ailerons near the wingtips do that.
wrong.C: Pressure in the cabin is a separate feature of modern jets.
wrong.D: The text says the engines generate thrust.

HIGH.stem: In the article, what does the word precision mean?
options: Great speed in the sky
Great weight on the wings
Great care and exactness
Great noise in the cabin
HIGH.why: Pilots adjust moving surfaces with precision, which means they control the plane exactly.

wrong.A: Speed is a different idea from exact control.
wrong.B: Weight does not describe how pilots control the plane.
wrong.D: The text does not link precision with noise.

HIGH.stem: What can you infer from the last paragraph?
options: Flying is too old to change
Engineers think flight can still improve
Planes are now as light as possible
Safe flights are very rare today
HIGH.why: Engineers keep studying flight to make future planes lighter, quieter, and better.

wrong.A: The text says engineers keep trying new ideas.
wrong.C: Engineers still hope to make planes lighter.
wrong.D: Safe flights happen every day, so they are not rare.

HIGH.stem: What pushes a wing upward as the plane gains speed?
options: Air getting hotter near the cockpit
Wood and cloth on the wings
A change in the pitch of the engines
A difference in air pressure
HIGH.why: The text says air flows over and under each wing and this difference in pressure pushes the wing upward.

wrong.A: The text does not mention heat near the cockpit.
wrong.B: Wood and cloth were used for the first Wright plane's frame, not to push the wing up.
wrong.C: Engines make thrust, a forward push, not lift.
